slides.body: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery.
That is what force is for. It is also the one push that can remove other people's commits from a branch, including commits you have never seen.
So today has three layers. Plain --force and what it destroys.
Here's what you'll walk away with.

slides.body: git push --force 🔴 DANGEROUS.
What it changes: the ref on the server, and your remote-tracking ref.
What it can destroy: every commit on the server's branch that is not in your history, including commits you have never seen.
Try it now. Thirty seconds, on paper.
How to preview, and here's the answer: git fetch, then git log --oneline HEAD..origin/<branch> lists exactly the commits that would be dropped.

How to recover: the old tip survives in any clone that had it, a teammate's branch or the reflog of anybody's remote-tracking ref, and, until the server's garbage collection removes it, as an unreachable object on the server …
When it is appropriate: on a branch that only you use, such as your own pull request branch after a rebase, or in a coordinated history rewrite.

The first root-cause box of section 12.8.
slides.text:
Observed behavior : git push --force-with-lease overwrote a teammate's commit that I had never looked at.
Git state         : refs/remotes/origin/feature/prompt-cache had been moved to the teammate's commit
                    by a fetch; my local branch did not contain that commit.
Mechanism         : the lease compares the server's ref with my remote-tracking ref. After the fetch
                    they were equal, so the condition "nothing changed since I looked" was true.
Root cause        : a remote-tracking ref records what my clone has fetched, not what I have seen or
                    integrated. Any fetch renews the lease.
Why Git does this : the remote-tracking ref is the only record Git has of "the state I based my work on",
                    and the manual says so and calls the forms without an explicit value experimental.
Correct fix       : restore the overwritten commit (below); nothing can be un-pushed.
Prevention        : --force-with-lease together with --force-if-includes (or push.useForceIfIncludes=true),
                    or the explicit --force-with-lease=<ref>:<commit>; and never rewrite a branch
                    that someone else pushes to without telling them.

The second root-cause box of section 12.8.
slides.text:
Observed behavior : after a teammate's forced push, git pull --rebase succeeded and my commit vanished
                    from the branch.
Git state         : I had pushed that commit earlier, so the reflog of origin/feature/prompt-cache
                    contains it ("update by push"). The server's branch was then replaced.
Mechanism         : pull --rebase replays only the commits after the fork point, and the fork point is
                    found through the reflog of the remote-tracking ref (git merge-base --fork-point).
                    It was my own pushed commit, so nothing was left to replay.
Root cause        : Git cannot tell "the upstream removed this commit on purpose" from "someone
                    overwrote it by accident". The reflog says only: it was upstream once, it is not now.
Why Git does this : without the rule, everyone downstream of a deliberately rebased branch would
                    re-apply the commits that the upstream had dropped.
Correct fix       : the commit is in my reflog; cherry-pick it onto the new tip and push.
Prevention        : after any "(forced update)" line, look before integrating:
                    git log --oneline --graph HEAD @{u}. Do not pull on a branch that others rewrite.

slides.body: Five mistakes to watch for.

items: Treating --force-with-lease as "safe force". Root cause: the bare lease compares the server with your remote-tracking ref, and any fetch, including one you never looked at, renews it.
Using plain --force on a branch you have not fetched. Root cause: nothing is checked, so commits you have never seen are dropped and your own clone holds no copy.

Running git pull --rebase after a "(forced update)" line. Root cause: the fork point comes from the reflog of the remote-tracking ref, so commits you had already pushed are treated as removed upstream and are not replayed.
Believing a forced push removes a commit from the server. Root cause: the old commits remain as unreachable objects until garbage collection, and a server may hand them out by full ID.
Looking for the overwritten commit in the server's reflog. Root cause: core.logAllRefUpdates defaults to false in a bare repository, so a plain bare server has none.

slides.body: On GitHub, according to the documentation, "Block force pushes" is enabled by default in a new ruleset, and classic branch protection rules disable force pushes by default.
Your turn. Do Lab 7.4, "When --force-with-lease saves you and when it does not", in lab-manual/m07-remotes.md.

slides.body: Read section 12.8 of Chapter 12.
Then close the book and write the lease-defeating sequence from memory as a timeline with three columns: you, the server, the teammate.
Today you answered the CTO: the lease was renewed by a fetch nobody read, and the lost commit was in three places you can now name.

beats.text: The CTO's question, word for word from the chapter: "Someone force-pushed with the 'safe' option, --force-with-lease, and a colleague's commit still disappeared from the shared branch. How, and where is that commit now?"
beats.tele: The CTO's question, word for word from the chapter: "Someone force-pushed with the 'safe' option, `--force-with-lease`, and a colleague's commit still disappeared from the shared branch. How, and where is that commit now?"

beats.text: The short answer: the lease was satisfied by a fetch that nobody looked at, and the commit still sits in places you can name. The long answer is this video. You will build the losing sequence step by step, watch the guard pass when it should have refused, and then find the commit in three different places. Keep count of those places.
beats.tele: The short answer: the lease was satisfied by a fetch that nobody looked at, and the commit still sits in places you can name. The long answer is this video. You will build the losing sequence step by step, watch the guard pass when it should have refused, and then find the commit in three different places. Keep count of those places.

beats.text: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. A push asks the server to move one of its branches to a commit of yours. In the last video a push was refused because it was not a fast-forward, and the fix was to integrate. But sometimes you don't want to integrate. You rebased your own pull request branch. You squashed two work-in-progress commits into one. The server's history is the old one and you want it replaced.
beats.tele: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. A push asks the server to move one of its branches to a commit of yours. In the last video a push was refused because it was not a fast-forward, and the fix was to integrate. But sometimes you don't want to integrate. You rebased your own pull request branch. You squashed two work-in-progress commits into one. The server's history is the old one and you want it replaced.

beats.text: That is what force is for. It is also the one push that can remove other people's commits from a branch, including commits you have never seen.
beats.tele: That is what force is for. It is also the one push that can remove other people's commits from a branch, including commits you have never seen.

beats.text: So today has three layers. Plain --force and what it destroys. --force-with-lease, what it compares, and the exact sequence that defeats it. And the two stronger forms that survive that sequence. Then you cross to the teammate's clone and see what the rewrite does there, because the damage has a second act that surprises people even more than the first.
beats.tele: So today has three layers. Plain `--force` and what it destroys. `--force-with-lease`, what it compares, and the exact sequence that defeats it. And the two stronger forms that survive that sequence. Then you cross to the teammate's clone and see what the rewrite does there, because the damage has a second act that surprises people even more than the first.

beats.text: Recall the seven steps of a push. Step 2 was the client rule: an existing branch may only be fast-forwarded. A forced push tells step 2 to skip the fast-forward test. The server's ref is set to your commit, and whatever it named before is no longer reachable from that ref.

beats.text: git push --force 🔴 DANGEROUS. It's also spelled -f, or a plus sign before one refspec. This is the first dangerous command of the video, so the five answers come before anything is run. Twig looks worried, and with a red label on screen, fairly so.
beats.tele: `git push --force` 🔴 DANGEROUS. It's also spelled `-f`, or a plus sign before one refspec. This is the first dangerous command of the video, so the five answers come before anything is run. Twig looks worried, and with a red label on screen, fairly so.

beats.text: What it changes: the ref on the server, and your remote-tracking ref.
beats.tele: What it changes: the ref on the server, and your remote-tracking ref.

beats.text: What it can destroy: every commit on the server's branch that is not in your history, including commits you have never seen. A default bare server has no reflog, so it keeps no pointer to them.
beats.tele: What it can destroy: every commit on the server's branch that is not in your history, including commits you have never seen. A default bare server has no reflog, so it keeps no pointer to them.

beats.text: Try it now. Thirty seconds, on paper. You have fetched. Write a git log command that lists the commits a forced push of your branch would drop. Then say it out loud.
beats.tele: Try it now. Thirty seconds, on paper. You have fetched. Write a `git log` command that lists the commits a forced push of your branch would drop. Then say it out loud.

beats.text: How to preview, and here's the answer: git fetch, then git log --oneline HEAD..origin/<branch> lists exactly the commits that would be dropped. git push --dry-run --force prints the server's current commit ID to the left of the three dots.
beats.tele: How to preview, and here's the answer: `git fetch`, then `git log --oneline HEAD..origin/<branch>` lists exactly the commits that would be dropped. `git push --dry-run --force` prints the server's current commit ID to the left of the three dots.

beats.text: How to recover: the old tip survives in any clone that had it, a teammate's branch or the reflog of anybody's remote-tracking ref, and, until the server's garbage collection removes it, as an unreachable object on the server, one that no ref leads to any more. Push it back.
beats.tele: How to recover: the old tip survives in any clone that had it, a teammate's branch or the reflog of anybody's remote-tracking ref, and, until the server's garbage collection removes it, as an unreachable object on the server, one that no ref leads to any more. Push it back.

beats.text: When it is appropriate: on a branch that only you use, such as your own pull request branch after a rebase, or in a coordinated history rewrite. Then use a lease.
beats.tele: When it is appropriate: on a branch that only you use, such as your own pull request branch after a rebase, or in a coordinated history rewrite. Then use a lease.

beats.text: Now the lease. --force-with-lease means: force only if the server is where I think it is. The bare form says "overwrite only if the server's branch still equals my remote-tracking ref".
beats.tele: Now the lease. `--force-with-lease` means: force only if the server is where I think it is. The bare form says "overwrite only if the server's branch still equals my remote-tracking ref".

beats.text: Quick quiz. While you work, your editor quietly runs git fetch. Does your lease, A, stay as it was, or B, get renewed? Your answer?
beats.tele: Quick quiz. While you work, your editor quietly runs `git fetch`. Does your lease, A, stay as it was, or B, get renewed? Your answer?

says: Your editor quietly runs git fetch. What happens to the lease?

beats.text: It's B, and there is the weakness, in the definition. The lease does not compare the server with what you have seen. It compares the server with your remote-tracking ref. Anything that moves that ref renews the lease: an editor's auto-fetch, a scheduled job, or you in another terminal.

beats.text: --force-if-includes adds a second condition: the tip of the remote-tracking ref must be reachable from some entry in the reflog of your local branch, meaning your branch contained that commit at some time. The setting push.useForceIfIncludes=true turns it on for every lease.
beats.tele: `--force-if-includes` adds a second condition: the tip of the remote-tracking ref must be reachable from some entry in the reflog of your local branch, meaning your branch contained that commit at some time. The setting `push.useForceIfIncludes=true` turns it on for every lease.

beats.text: And the explicit form, --force-with-lease=<ref>:<expect>, ignores the remote-tracking ref and compares the server with a commit you name.
beats.tele: And the explicit form, `--force-with-lease=<ref>:<expect>`, ignores the remote-tracking ref and compares the server with a commit you name.

beats.text: When not to force at all: on a branch that someone else pushes to, unless you have told them. And never as a routine undo on main. The textbook marks that as outdated advice: tutorials that teach "git reset --hard, then git push -f" teach the one habit in this chapter that loses other people's work. Undo published commits with git revert.
beats.tele: When not to force at all: on a branch that someone else pushes to, unless you have told them. And never as a routine undo on `main`. The textbook marks that as outdated advice: tutorials that teach "`git reset --hard`, then `git push -f`" teach the one habit in this chapter that loses other people's work. Undo published commits with `git revert`.

beats.text: A picture helps. The textbook's model for the lease is the compare-and-swap of optimistic locking: "set the branch to my commit only if it still has the value I last read".
beats.tele: A picture helps. The textbook's model for the lease is the compare-and-swap of optimistic locking: "set the branch to my commit only if it still has the value I last read".

beats.text: It breaks at the word "I". Your Git does the reading, and a fetch that you never looked at refreshes the value. In a database, you read a row, you compute, you write back with the old value as a condition. Here, something else can re-read the row on your behalf, silently, between your computing and your writing, and the condition then holds for a value you never used.

beats.text: So keep two things apart that feel like one: what my clone has fetched, and what I have seen or integrated. A remote-tracking ref records the first. Only your branch's own history records the second, and that is exactly what --force-if-includes consults. This is today's case, a little ahead of the demo: a fetch has put origin/feature/prompt-cache on 833bc8a, and your branch, at 1a1fa49, has never contained that commit.

beats.text: Pull with rebase replays only the commits after the fork point, and the fork point is found through the reflog of the remote-tracking ref. So nothing was left to replay. If that feels unfair to Asha, hold on: the root-cause box says why Git does it.

beats.text: Under protocol version 2, the default, a plain Git server hands out any object it has when asked by full ID. An abbreviation is not accepted, and under protocol version 0 the request is refused. This is a recovery route for as long as the object exists. It is also one reason why a forced push does not remove a leaked secret from a server.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Treating --force-with-lease as "safe force". Root cause: the bare lease compares the server with your remote-tracking ref, and any fetch, including one you never looked at, renews it.
beats.tele: Treating `--force-with-lease` as "safe force". Root cause: the bare lease compares the server with your remote-tracking ref, and any fetch, including one you never looked at, renews it.

beats.text: Using plain --force on a branch you have not fetched. Root cause: nothing is checked, so commits you have never seen are dropped and your own clone holds no copy.
beats.tele: Using plain `--force` on a branch you have not fetched. Root cause: nothing is checked, so commits you have never seen are dropped and your own clone holds no copy.

beats.text: Running git pull --rebase after a "(forced update)" line. Root cause: the fork point comes from the reflog of the remote-tracking ref, so commits you had already pushed are treated as removed upstream and are not replayed.
beats.tele: Running `git pull --rebase` after a "(forced update)" line. Root cause: the fork point comes from the reflog of the remote-tracking ref, so commits you had already pushed are treated as removed upstream and are not replayed.

beats.text: Believing a forced push removes a commit from the server. Root cause: the old commits remain as unreachable objects until garbage collection, and a server may hand them out by full ID.
beats.tele: Believing a forced push removes a commit from the server. Root cause: the old commits remain as unreachable objects until garbage collection, and a server may hand them out by full ID.

beats.text: Looking for the overwritten commit in the server's reflog. Root cause: core.logAllRefUpdates defaults to false in a bare repository, so a plain bare server has none.
beats.tele: Looking for the overwritten commit in the server's reflog. Root cause: `core.logAllRefUpdates` defaults to false in a bare repository, so a plain bare server has none.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. The textbook gives a routine for rewriting a branch that is already published. One: fetch and read git status -sb. Two: mark the old tip, git branch backup/<name>. Three: rewrite. Four: push with --force-with-lease=<name>:backup/<name>. Five: tell everyone who has the branch what to do next. And set push.useForceIfIncludes=true once, for the days you forget the explicit form.
beats.tele: Now, out of the lab. The textbook gives a routine for rewriting a branch that is already published. One: fetch and read `git status -sb`. Two: mark the old tip, `git branch backup/<name>`. Three: rewrite. Four: push with `--force-with-lease=<name>:backup/<name>`. Five: tell everyone who has the branch what to do next. And set `push.useForceIfIncludes=true` once, for the days you forget the explicit form.

beats.text: Picture an evaluation team where two people share a long-running experiment branch. One of them rebases it on Friday evening using that routine, minus step five. On Monday the other runs git pull --rebase out of habit. It says "Successfully rebased". Their Friday commit is gone from the branch and nothing was red. Step five is not politeness. It is the only control for the second root-cause box.

beats.text: On GitHub, according to the documentation, "Block force pushes" is enabled by default in a new ruleset, and classic branch protection rules disable force pushes by default. GitHub offers no reflog that Git can query, but its Activity view lists force pushes and offers a comparison for each entry, and its troubleshooting page gives the plain-Git answer: ask a collaborator who still has the commit to push it to a new branch. The interface changes. The documentation is the reference.

beats.text: Q203: "Why does --force-with-lease exist?"
beats.tele: Q203: "Why does `--force-with-lease` exist?"

beats.text: Answer out loud first. A strong answer starts from the problem, what plain force does not check, and states the lease as a condition on two specific refs. It does not stop there: it names the assumption the condition rests on and one ordinary event that breaks it. It then gives the stronger forms and what each compares instead.
